title: Evidence & measurement
blurb: The traps that wreck analytics: selection, small numbers, shifting mixes, broken series, proxies and measures that become targets.

cards.prompt: An intervention targets the 10 sites with the most incidents last quarter, and incidents drop the next quarter. Why isn't that evidence it worked?
cards.answer: Regression to the mean. Sites picked because they had an extreme period tend to look more typical the next period whether or not anything was done. You need a comparison group selected the same way, or longer pre-intervention trends.
points: Selection on an extreme value
Regression to the mean happens without any intervention
Comparison group chosen the same way, or longer pre-trends
cards.source: Standard; see Campbell & Ross (1968) on the Connecticut speeding crackdown

cards.answer: The more any quantitative social indicator is used for social decision-making, the more subject it will be to corruption pressures and the more apt it will be to distort and corrupt the social processes it is intended to monitor.
cards.why: Close relative of Goodhart's law (popular form, after Strathern): when a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure.
cards.source: Donald T. Campbell, Assessing the Impact of Planned Social Change (1979)

cards.prompt: What is the identifying assumption of difference-in-differences?
cards.answer: Parallel trends: absent the treatment, the treated and comparison groups would have changed by the same amount.
cards.why: Check the pre-period trends, and look for anything else that changed at the same time.

cards.prompt: Why do 'top 10 by rate' rankings of branches, schools or neighborhoods keep featuring the smallest ones, and what do you do about it?
cards.answer: Small denominators make rates noisy, so by chance small units fill both the top and the bottom of the ranking. Use funnel plots, empirical-Bayes shrinkage toward the overall rate, minimum denominators, or pooled years, and show the uncertainty.
points: Small denominators produce extreme rates in both directions
Funnel plots or shrinkage
Minimum denominators or pooled years
Show uncertainty
cards.source: Gelman & Price, All maps of parameter estimates are misleading (1999)

cards.prompt: An executive asks for 'the 10 worst locations for complaints' from raw counts. What do you ask and adjust before you send a list?
cards.answer: Normalize by an exposure measure (customers, units, visits) rather than using raw counts. Raise detection bias: complaints reflect who complains and where staff look, not only where problems are. Small numbers make rankings unstable, so pool time or shrink the rates. Pin down the time window and which complaints count (type, severity, open or closed). Ask what decision the list is for, and present it with uncertainty and context.
points: Normalize by exposure
Detection and reporting bias
Small-number instability
Define the window and the categories
Ask what decision it informs; show uncertainty

cards.prompt: Average resolution time improved in every region, yet the organization-wide average got worse. How?
cards.answer: Simpson's paradox. The mix shifted: more cases now come from regions or case types with long resolution times, so the weighted average rises even though every subgroup improved. Report stratified figures or standardize the mix.
points: Composition shift between subgroups
Weighted average can move against every subgroup
Stratify or standardize

cards.prompt: Inspections, complaints and enforcement records all count something. What do they actually measure, and what follows?
cards.answer: They record the organization's process: where it looked, who reported, what staff chose to write down. That mixes the underlying problem with effort and reporting behavior. More inspectors or an easier complaint channel raise counts with no change in the problem. Model or at least report effort alongside the counts, and be wary of comparing areas with different detection.
points: Administrative data measures the process, not just the phenomenon
Counts move with effort and reporting behavior
Report effort alongside counts
Detection differences confound comparisons

cards.prompt: A metric's definition, source system or coverage changes partway through a time series. What do you do?
cards.answer: Treat it as a break in the series, not a trend. Mark the break on every chart, run old and new methods in parallel for an overlap period if you can, and either bridge (back-cast) with the overlap or report the two segments separately.
cards.why: Example: US national crime statistics broke in 2021 when the FBI moved to an incident-based system and many agencies hadn't converted.
points: A method change is a break, not a trend
Annotate the break
Parallel run for an overlap period
Bridge with the overlap, or report segments separately

cards.prompt: Two estimates have overlapping 95% confidence intervals. Does that mean the difference isn't significant?
cards.answer: No. Test the difference itself. For independent estimates its standard error is sqrt(SE1² + SE2²), which is smaller than SE1 + SE2, so intervals can overlap while the difference is still significant.
cards.source: Schenker & Gentleman, On judging the significance of differences by examining the overlap between confidence intervals (2001)

cards.prompt: A field classifies records for one administrative purpose, such as a land-use code for tax assessment. Why is it risky to use it to count a real-world state, like vacant buildings?
cards.answer: The code answers the question its process asks, not yours. An abandoned house usually keeps its residential code, and codes lag reality. Treat it as a proxy, look for direct signals of the state you care about, validate the proxy against ground truth, and define the target state explicitly.
points: Codes answer their own process's question
Classification lags and diverges from reality
Seek direct signals; triangulate sources
Validate the proxy against ground truth
Define the target state explicitly
